title: PTSDee

jokes.text: Jesus Christ, Frank, you just killed a kid! / Eh.
jokes.setup: Frank apparently shoots a child in what we assume is a real warzone scenario
jokes.punchline: Frank's single-syllable shrug 'Eh.' reveals total moral indifference — and the reveal that this is a video game is still seconds away
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'Eh.' is perfect character economy — maximum moral bankrupcy in one syllable. It works on first watch as dark shock and on rewatch knowing it's a video game, the indifference is STILL the joke. Classic Frank. The structure is excellent: big accusation, tiny deflating response.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Jesus Christ, Frank, you just killed a kid!

jokes.text: Now, is he blowing someone? What is happening?
jokes.setup: Mac tries to give CPR to a downed character in a video game
jokes.punchline: Dennis, watching from outside, has no context and interprets the button-mashing animation as sexual
jokes.explanation: Good confusion comedy — Dennis's detached, clinical framing ('Is he blowing someone?') is very on-brand. The joke earns its laugh from the absurd misread but isn't transcendent.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Eh.

jokes.text: They've been playing this for three days straight, wandering around the bar, blowing kids, doing whatever.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks how long Frank and Mac have been absorbed in the video game
jokes.punchline: Three days straight — with the callback to the CPR-as-oral-sex reading — framed as a mundane update
jokes.explanation: The 'three days' escalation is good, and 'blowing kids' as a throwaway callback lands. Charlie's matter-of-fact delivery of absurd facts is a show staple that works here.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Now, is he blowing someone? What is happening?

jokes.text: Is this where we're headed? I mean, as a world? As a society?
jokes.setup: Mac and Frank are zombie-deep in a war video game for 72+ hours
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a mock-philosophical societal lament about two idiots playing video games, performed with his characteristic narcissistic gravitas
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis self-important monologue applied to the most trivial situation. The gap between his grandiosity and the subject (a video game) is the joke. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: three straight days... No. No, they've just been wandering around the bar, blowing kids, doing whatever they're doing

jokes.text: I meet myself a Channing Tatum and suddenly it's gross?
jokes.setup: Dee brags about hooking up with a hot stripper soldier; Dennis and Charlie say 'gross'
jokes.punchline: Dee compares the stripper to Channing Tatum — revealing her delusion that this is a romantic conquest rather than what it obviously is
jokes.explanation: Dee's self-delusion is a core character trait and this is a solid instance of it. The double standard she calls out (rightly!) is immediately undercut by her ridiculous comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No. No, they've just been wandering around the bar, blowing kids, doing whatever they're doing, you know?

jokes.text: A what... a charming taint man?
jokes.setup: Dee says 'Channing Tatum' and Frank mishears it
jokes.punchline: 'Charming taint man' — Frank's mishearing creates an accidentally obscene non-sequitur that is somehow worse than the original name
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best quick jokes. 'Charming taint man' is an inspired mishearing — it sounds just plausible enough phonetically while being maximally gross. Frank's bewilderment is pitch-perfect character work. High quotability and the economy (four words) is excellent. Narrowly misses 8+ on craft due to being a one-off rather than structurally integrated, but it's very close.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: A what... a charming taint man? What words is she trying to say?

jokes.text: Both of us wept tears of joy during the sex
jokes.setup: Dee is building up her romantic hookup with the stripper
jokes.punchline: She claims the sex was so meaningful they both cried — which is immediately revealed to be untrue for his side
jokes.explanation: Setup joke that pays off magnificently when Mike reveals he was crying because he hit rock bottom, not from joy. Good structural setup with strong payoff incoming. On its own, moderately funny; rewatch bonus because you know the punchline is coming.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, then say G.I. Joe, don't make up a name.

jokes.text: He-he plays G.I. Joe. / G.I. Joe! G.I. Joe's the shit. / Well, then say G.I. Joe, don't make up a name.
jokes.setup: Frank has no idea who Channing Tatum is; Charlie explains he plays G.I. Joe
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately embraces this ('G.I. Joe's the shit!') but then scolds Dee for using 'made-up names' rather than just saying 'G.I. Joe' — as if the character name is the real one
jokes.explanation: Frank's logic is internally consistent and completely backwards — he thinks the fictional character name is correct and the actor's real name is a fake name. This is sharp character comedy showing Frank's particular brand of confident ignorance.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: we had this really amazing connection and the sex was so meaningful, both of us wept tears of joy.

jokes.text: So you have my watch? / Yeah. Just diving straight into that, huh?
jokes.setup: Dee has stolen Mike's watch to get him to come back; she's hoping for a romantic reunion
jokes.punchline: Mike immediately asks for his watch back with zero romantic interest, and Dee's sad 'just diving straight into that, huh?' signals her immediate deflation
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe setup — Dee's pathetic gambit is immediately exposed. The punchline is in Mike's total obliviousness and Dee's self-aware sad response. Functional cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Makes me want to throw up.

jokes.text: I was like, 'What's become of me?' All I do is strip all night, play video games all day, have meaningless sex with strangers. My own daughter won't even talk to me. And I realized I hit rock bottom. And that's why I was crying.
jokes.setup: Dee assumes Mike was emotionally moved by their intimate connection and wept tears of joy during sex
jokes.punchline: Mike was crying because he realized SHE was his rock bottom — having sex with her was the catalyst for his self-reckoning
jokes.explanation: Structurally excellent misdirection. Dee told everyone he 'wept tears of joy' — the reveal that those were tears of despair at hitting rock bottom (with her) is a devastating, well-earned punchline. The structure mirrors and subverts the setup perfectly. The fact that he lists all these terrible things and lands on 'sex with a stranger' — implicitly meaning Dee — is brutal and characteristically cruel to Dee in the show's tradition.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I think the guy's coming by because you stole his watch.

jokes.text: Um... I don't remember your name.
jokes.setup: Mike has just shared an emotionally raw revelation about rock bottom to Dee's face
jokes.punchline: He doesn't even remember her name, completing the humiliation
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. After the devastating rock-bottom reveal, the capper 'I don't remember your name' is the final twist of the knife. It's one of those jokes that's simple but lands hard because of placement and timing. The beat before Dee quietly says 'Dee' makes it land even harder.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Just diving straight into that, huh?

jokes.text: You know what I am? I'm a rock. Dee is a rock. In fact, I'm the type of gal who makes men's lives better.
jokes.setup: Dee is in a talking-head confessional, responding to being told she's someone's rock bottom
jokes.punchline: Her delusional reframing — 'I'm a rock, I make men's lives better' — is immediately contradicted by everything we've seen
jokes.explanation: Dee's self-delusion confessional is a show staple. 'I'm a rock' becomes a running gag anchor for the episode. Good character comedy, well-delivered, though not surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: What's become of me? all I do is I strip all night, I play video games all day, I have meaningless sex with strangers. My own daughter won't even talk to me

jokes.text: Hey-o! You guys mind if I shower in that leaky urinal again?
jokes.setup: Dee's confessional claims she 'makes men's lives better'
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately wanders in asking to shower in the urinal — a perfect real-time rebuttal of her claim, and a visual gag implying just how low-rent the gang's lifestyle is
jokes.explanation: Structurally brilliant juxtaposition comedy. Dee claims she makes men's lives better, and instantaneously Mac — a grown man — asks to shower in a bar urinal. The timing is what elevates this from a decent gag to an excellent one. The specificity ('leaky urinal') and Mac's obliviousness are both perfect. Earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: And that's why I was crying.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Right, yeah. Yeah. But don't-don't take it personally.

jokes.text: Well, that... Don't count that. That's not a good example.
jokes.setup: Mac's urinal shower request perfectly contradicts Dee's claim
jokes.punchline: Dee's flustered, self-aware attempt to discredit the evidence while remaining in confessional mode
jokes.explanation: Good callback capper. Dee's self-aware damage control is funny precisely because she can't stop the evidence from mounting. Pairs well with #12 as a beat-two follow-through.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Um... I don't remember your name.

jokes.text: Goddamn it, Charlie, we're 30 minutes late, man. / I'm so sorry I cut your back so many times, man. / What happened? / I was nervous, dude. I've never cut such a muscular back.
jokes.setup: Dennis needed Charlie to check for moles and trim unsightly hairs before his stripping debut
jokes.punchline: Charlie cut Dennis's back multiple times while grooming him, apparently out of nervousness at the musculature — which Dennis accepts as a compliment
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Charlie nervously slashed up Dennis's back is funny on its own, but the best bit is Dennis hearing 'I've never cut such a muscular back' and being completely mollified. Pure Dennis vanity. Good character-specific comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Rock bottom? Me? how about when your daughter stopped talking to you... Maybe that was your rock bottom, okay? I'm not rock bottom. You know what I am? I'm a rock.

jokes.text: Mac's banged up over a goddamn video game. And then he has sex with one disgusting bird. Come on, man, that's not trauma. That's not real trauma. That's insulting to people who have experienced real trauma.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie are critiquing everyone's 'trauma'
jokes.punchline: Dennis is appalled that the stripper's lifestyle constitutes 'trauma' — with zero self-awareness that he's about to voluntarily enter the same profession
jokes.explanation: Dennis's moral indignation about fake trauma is funny given the context. 'One disgusting bird' is a classic Dennis-ism. The dramatic irony of him disparaging stripping while about to become a stripper is good structural comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Rock bottom? Me? Uh, hey, buddy, how about when your daughter stopped talking to you... Maybe that was your rock bottom, okay?

jokes.text: And-and you, too. I mean, like, you know, what happened with you... with Ms. Klinsky, the librarian. I mean, you were raped. / Ah. No. St... / And tha-that's got to affect you. That's trauma. / Will you stop? / A woman can't rape a guy. / An older woman can rape a younger... / Doesn't matter.
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to point to real trauma in Dennis's life
jokes.punchline: Dennis flatly insists 'a woman can't rape a guy' — a classic demonstration of Dennis's disordered thinking about sex and power
jokes.explanation: Dennis's reflexive dismissal of his own victimization is a character-specific joke that also works as dark commentary on gendered thinking about assault. The show uses Dennis's psychology to critique this attitude rather than endorse it. Good character integration — only Dennis would respond this way.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Hey-o! You guys mind if I shower in that leaky urinal again?

jokes.text: You'll do what? / I'll strip. Yeah. / Huh. I didn't realize you were talking about that.
jokes.setup: Dennis has been talking abstractly about not being defeated and taking up a 'mantle'
jokes.punchline: He announces 'I'll strip' — which Charlie (and the audience) didn't see coming from the conversation's framing — and his genuine enthusiasm ('frankly I'm disappointed I didn't think of it before') is immediately deflated by Charlie's oblivious non-reaction
jokes.explanation: Minor misdirection gag. Dennis's announcement is a slight surprise and Charlie's flat 'didn't realize you were talking about that' is a decent deflation. Functional but not memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Well, that... Don't count that. That's not a good example.

jokes.text: I need you to have a look at my back, you know, make sure there's no moles or, like, unsightly hairs, bumps, zits, you know, that kind of thing. And then, you know, get after it.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Charlie to 'have his back' before stripping
jokes.punchline: His clinical list of back problems — moles, hairs, bumps, zits — combined with 'get after it' reveals his vanity and total comfort asking Charlie to do unpleasant grooming tasks
jokes.explanation: Dennis's self-maintenance routine being outsourced to Charlie is a funny dynamic. The list itself is the joke — 'moles, unsightly hairs, bumps, zits' — and 'get after it' as a casual command to essentially be his groomer is very Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Goddamn it, Frank, you shot a woman.

jokes.text: Dennis asks Charlie to be his 'bag boy' — carrying lotions, oils, scents, razors
jokes.setup: Charlie agrees to 'be Dennis's boy' as a stripping assistant
jokes.punchline: Dennis elaborates the role into a personal valet carrying his beauty products — 'my lotions, my oils, my scents, my razors' — Charlie agreeing while Dennis is oblivious to how demeaning this is
jokes.explanation: The list of Dennis's vanity products ('lotions, oils, scents, razors') sketches his self-care obsession economically. Charlie's 'Cool, man. Chill, chill.' while agreeing to be a valet is a good beat. Part of a running gag about Dennis treating Charlie as a subordinate.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: you were raised by a woman who was basically a prostitute.

jokes.text: No! Baba! Mother! Oh, shit! Oh, no, man! I'm so sorry, man. Hey, son. Dad?! What are you doing here? How did you get in the game? Guess we won't be having that catch after all. / You were gonna have a catch with me? / I was, but... you killed me, son. I love...
jokes.setup: Mac is playing the war video game and shoots someone; it turns out to be Frank — who has somehow entered the game world in Mac's dream/game space
jokes.punchline: Frank appears as Mac's father in the game, announces they 'won't be having that catch' because Mac killed him, and dies mid-declaration of love — leaving Mac screaming 'Who do you love?'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sequences. The game-dad-dream fusion is inventive and Mac's specific need — the catch that never happened — is a perfect character detail. 'Guess we won't be having that catch after all' as a dying man's words is brilliantly tragic-comic. The unfinished 'I love...' leaving Mac screaming 'Who do you love?!' is a devastating and funny bit of unresolved parental longing. Strong originality, great structure.

dialogue.line: stripper guy is traumatized because he gets to take his clothes off in front of a bunch of horny ladies.

jokes.text: Kid's a mess.
jokes.setup: Mac has just had an emotional breakdown about the video game and left the room
jokes.punchline: Frank watches him go and delivers a flat 'Kid's a mess' — total detachment from Mac's psychological crisis, treating it as a minor behavioral observation
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words, complete character encapsulation. Frank's total dismissal of genuine psychological distress as 'a mess' is very Frank. The brevity is what makes it land; any more words would ruin it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: what happened with you... with Ms. Klinsky, the librarian. I mean, you were raped.

jokes.text: Who do girls want to have sex with more than anybody else? / Jugglers. / Jug—? Dudes who can, like, juggle things.
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining his strip club persona concept and asks who girls most want to sleep with
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate, confident answer is 'jugglers' — not explained, not qualified, just stated as obvious fact
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup invites a straight answer — and Charlie's 'jugglers' is so confidently wrong, so specifically absurd, and so perfectly Charlie that it lands beautifully. The follow-up 'Dudes who can, like, juggle things. You know, with the fire sticks and the balls.' — explaining the obvious — makes it even better. Pure Charlie absurdist logic delivered as wisdom. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: A woman can't rape a guy.

jokes.text: No, they don't want to have sex with a juggler. They want to have sex with their dads. / Weird. / Yeah, it is weird.
jokes.setup: Dennis corrects Charlie's juggler theory
jokes.punchline: Dennis's confident alternative — 'their dads' — is stated so matter-of-factly that Charlie just says 'weird' and Dennis agrees, as if that settles it
jokes.explanation: Dennis delivering deeply weird psychosexual 'wisdom' with total authority, and Charlie's 'Weird. / Yeah, it is weird.' being the only response needed — this exchange is Sunny at its best. The mutual acknowledgment of weirdness with zero follow-up concern is hilarious. The deadpan delivery elevates what could be a cheap shock joke into something with real comic structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I need you to get my back.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, uh, you want me to strip with you?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, oh, no, no, no, no, no. I just literally need you to have a look at my back

jokes.text: Oh, okay, cool. Oh, and I'm your boy. / Well, no. What? Why would you be my boy?
jokes.setup: Dennis explains his 'Dad' stripper character; Charlie immediately tries to insert himself as 'the Boy'
jokes.punchline: Charlie has misconstrued an earlier throwaway comment ('you be my boy') as a formal role in the stripping act
jokes.explanation: Charlie's complete earnestness about inserting himself into the act is funny, and Dennis's confused exasperation is on-brand. Functional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No! Baba! Mother!

jokes.text: Oh, you said I was gonna be your boy 'cause I have daddy trauma, and then I didn't realize I was gonna be your boy in there, but that works great.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks why Charlie would be his boy in the stripping act
jokes.punchline: Charlie explains his convoluted logic involving daddy trauma as qualification for the role, delivered as if this is completely reasonable
jokes.explanation: Charlie's self-referential trauma logic is funny but a little tangled. The delivery saves it — his earnest belief that 'daddy trauma' is a relevant professional credential for stripping is very Charlie.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dad?! What are you doing here? Guess we... won't be having that catch after all.

jokes.text: Are you gonna stand out here and talk like little bitches, or are you gonna come inside and take your dicks out for money?
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie are bickering outside the strip club about their roles
jokes.punchline: The manager cuts through their nonsense with this magnificently blunt ultimatum
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation. The manager's total lack of patience for their posturing — 'talk like little bitches or take your dicks out for money' — is both blunt and structurally satisfying as a punctuation mark on a scene of overthinking. Highly quotable, great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac's Dad
dialogue.line: you killed me, son. I... love...

jokes.text: Daddy? / Just don't call me Daddy.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just declared he's a 'dad' stripper character and walked in confidently
jokes.punchline: The first thing a customer calls him is 'Daddy' — which he immediately, uncomfortably rejects, suggesting even he has limits
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic reversal. Dennis spent the entire preceding scene confident about his 'dad' persona and immediately recoils when someone actually calls him Daddy. The speed of the reversal and his genuine discomfort makes it land. Very economical — four words of setup, four words of punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dad, who do you love? Wait. Dad, who do you love? No, Dad! No!

jokes.text: Yeah, my generation... we drank our problems away. But since you softies like to talk about everything, I figured this was a good thing to do. A PTSD support group, Frank?
jokes.setup: Frank has taken Mac to a veterans PTSD support group
jokes.punchline: Frank's framing — 'you softies like to talk' — reveals he thinks the support group is for Mac's benefit while he openly scorns the concept of emotional processing
jokes.explanation: Frank's generational contempt for emotional processing is classic Frank, and 'stuff it down with brown' is his credo. Decent character comedy, sets up the PTSD group scene well.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: stuff it down with brown. That's the best way to deal with things.

jokes.text: I'm Frank. I've been around the block, seen some action. I was in 'Nam for a while. Private sector mostly. I did shoot a couple of dinks who tried to jack some sneakers off the factory floor. No big deal. I don't feel nothing about it. I'm just here to support my buddy.
jokes.setup: PTSD support group facilitator asks newcomers to introduce themselves
jokes.punchline: Frank introduces his 'Vietnam trauma' as shooting factory workers over stolen sneakers in a private-sector sweatshop — delivered with zero self-awareness — then waves it off as 'no big deal'
jokes.explanation: This is Frank at his darkest and most specific. The joke escalates beautifully: 'Nam' sounds like he's a vet, 'private sector' slightly reframes it, then 'shot some people for stealing sneakers from my factory' is a full reveal of corporate thuggery that Frank considers equivalent to wartime PTSD. 'I don't feel nothing about it' is the perfect cap. High character integration — only Frank could deliver this. The slur use reflects the show's intent to characterize Frank as morally repugnant, not to endorse it.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm so sorry I cut your back so many times, man. I was nervous, dude. I've never, like, cut such a muscular back.

jokes.text: Hello. I'm Dee. I'm a rock. I'm here with this guy. There was a bit of a mix-up about his military credentials, but whatever.
jokes.setup: Dee introduces herself to a veterans PTSD support group
jokes.punchline: Dee's self-identification as 'a rock,' combined with the breezy 'mix-up about his military credentials' (he's a fake vet), delivered to actual trauma survivors
jokes.explanation: Dee's running 'I'm a rock' claim being deployed in a totally inappropriate setting to actual veterans is funny. 'Mix-up about his military credentials' as the most casual way to describe bringing a fake veteran to a support group is a solid understatement.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Who do girls want to have sex with more than anybody else?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Jugglers.

jokes.text: Mac's being a pussy! He doesn't want to fight anymore! / I'm not being a pussy. I just don't want to kill women and children. / How do I get him to stop thinking of them as real people?
jokes.setup: Frank is at a PTSD support group for veterans and uses it to complain about Mac not wanting to continue the video game
jokes.punchline: Frank's framing of Mac's video game moral crisis as a tactical problem ('how do I get him to stop thinking of them as real people?') lands as both absurdist and genuinely dark
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Frank casually asking 'how do I get him to stop thinking of them as real people' in a room full of veterans with actual trauma is incredibly dark and funny. The question itself — which could be sinister in another context — is about a video game, but it lands as an accidental meditation on dehumanization. Great structure: the cringe of the setting, the specificity of the ask, and Mac's straight-man corrective.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: They want to have sex with their dads.

jokes.text: Mike's embarrassed about his dancing, and I just don't get that. I don't... How is that rock bottom behavior? Think of Channing Tatum. Can you please explain Channing Tatum to him?
jokes.setup: Dee is making her case in the PTSD group
jokes.punchline: Dee deploys the Channing Tatum reference again (now a running gag) as if 'explain Channing Tatum' is a reasonable therapeutic intervention
jokes.explanation: Decent callback that uses the Channing Tatum running gag but doesn't add much new. The image of Dee asking a PTSD group to 'explain Channing Tatum' is funny primarily from context.

dialogue.speaker: Strip Club Manager
dialogue.line: Are you gonna stand out here and talk like little bitches, or are you gonna come inside and take your dicks out for money?

jokes.text: Oh, yeah. He's G.I. Joe. / Beat it five times. / You want to play with me? / I'm actually trying to get away from that. / Well, what if he paid you? / Ten bucks an hour. / 20. / Deal.
jokes.setup: Dee brings up Channing Tatum/G.I. Joe; it turns into the PTSD group facilitator and Mac negotiating over video game wages in front of veterans
jokes.punchline: The facilitator immediately agrees to play the war game for $20/hour, completely abandoning his professional role — the speed and mercenary practicality of this is the punchline
jokes.explanation: The escalation from PTSD group to negotiating video game wages is absurdist brilliance. The facilitator's immediate '20' counteroffer and 'Deal' — happening in his own therapy session — is a great subversion of authority and setting. The speed of the negotiation is what makes it land; it's pure sitcom escalation executed well.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I did shoot a couple of dinks who tried to jack some sneakers off the factory floor. No big deal. I don't feel nothing about it.

jokes.text: You're out. Dishonorable discharge.
jokes.setup: Dee realizes she's been left out of the arrangement
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses her using military terminology — 'dishonorable discharge' — which is both contextually appropriate (they're at a veteran's group) and a perfect expression of Frank's contempt
jokes.explanation: Clean, economical dismissal. 'Dishonorable discharge' is a perfectly chosen phrase — situationally appropriate, deeply cutting, and very Frank. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Hello. I'm Dee. I'm a rock.

jokes.text: Hey, son. / Dad?! What are you doing here? I broke out of jail and came straight to see you. / Because you love me? / 'Cause I'm gonna kill you, son.
jokes.setup: Mac falls asleep in the PTSD meeting; dream sequence: a father figure appears and Mac asks if he came because he loves him
jokes.punchline: 'Cause I'm gonna kill you, son.' — the father-love-being-answered-with-murder-threat is a perfect subversion of Mac's desperate need for paternal approval
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes because it operates on multiple levels. The structure is a perfect misdirection: Mac's tragic longing for paternal love ('Because you love me?') receives the most brutal possible answer. It's dark comedy AND character comedy — Mac's dad issues have been a years-long running thread in the show, and this nightmare crystallizes it perfectly. The economy of the punchline ('Cause I'm gonna kill you, son') is superb. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and exceeds it in character depth.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Mac's being a pussy! He doesn't want to fight anymore! How do I get him to stop thinking of them as real people?

jokes.text: What...? What's happening? When did I get here? How long have I been asleep? / You got here, like, five minutes ago. You've been asleep for 35 seconds.
jokes.setup: Mac woke up from his nightmare completely disoriented
jokes.punchline: He's been asleep for 35 seconds — the elaborate nightmare happened in under a minute, emphasizing how deep his psychological deterioration is
jokes.explanation: The 35-second detail is a good punchline — it's specific enough to be funny (not 'a minute' but '35 seconds') and it perfectly illustrates Mac's psychological state. Dennis's flat delivery of the precise time is very much in his character.

dialogue.speaker: Mac's Dad
dialogue.line: 'Cause I'm gonna kill you, son.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh. Oh, no!

jokes.text: What war? / The war on women! Women, man! / There's a war on women? Can I get in on that? / Bro, it's been raging since the beginning of time, bro. And we're losing ground.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie announce they're going to 'win this war'
jokes.punchline: The 'war on women' framing — where the gang's stripping scheme is pitched as a battle they're LOSING — is a sharp piece of dark irony; Mac's eager 'can I get in on that?' makes it worse
jokes.explanation: The gang's oblivious appropriation of 'war on women' as a battle they're fighting against women (by stripping for them) is sharp political-subtext comedy. Mac's 'Can I get in on that?' is the topper — his eagerness to join a 'war on women' is played completely straight.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We're gonna win this war.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What war?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: The war on women! Women, man!

jokes.text: Uh, yeah, is youse Daddy and the Boy? / Oh, uh, y-yes, it is. Boy speaking.
jokes.setup: Dee is calling in a fake booking disguised with a terrible accent
jokes.punchline: Charlie, answering as 'the Boy,' formally identifies himself as 'Boy speaking' — treating the absurd persona as a professional title
jokes.explanation: 'Boy speaking' as a formal phone greeting is a funny bit of self-seriousness. Charlie's total commitment to the persona elevates a simple joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Of course I knew it was you. Who else does accents so poorly?

jokes.text: Of course I knew it was you. Who else does accents so poorly?
jokes.setup: Dee is shocked to be identified by Dennis through her disguised phone voice
jokes.punchline: Dennis's instant identification of her — 'who else does accents so poorly?' — is a great character-specific burn
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-delivered burn that's very true to the Dee/Dennis dynamic. The economy is excellent and it's the kind of throwaway that gets quoted. Dennis's withering precision is very in-character.

jokes.text: Young girl sorority girls. It's, like, age-appropriate for me, you know? Not like those perverted librarians.
jokes.setup: Dennis is pleased about the sorority party booking
jokes.punchline: Dennis refers to librarians who had sex with him as 'perverted' — inverting the predator/victim dynamic in a way that's deeply revealing of his psychology
jokes.explanation: Dennis calling the people who victimized him 'perverted' as if he was the standard-setter is a revealing character joke. It also ties back to the ongoing Ms. Klinsky thread while adding a new layer to Dennis's twisted self-image.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Is that made of cheese?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah.

dialogue.line: Why did you make a cheese lollipop?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It stinks.

jokes.text: It's amazing! I can't believe they have zombies on the final level! I love zombies. Ghouls, too. I love ghouls.
jokes.setup: Frank has been dragged away from the game to sleep; we expect him to wake up recovered
jokes.punchline: Frank wakes up still totally absorbed, immediately excited about zombies and ghouls — he has not had a moment of reflection
jokes.explanation: 'I love ghouls, too' as an addendum is the best part — the specificity of Frank loving ghouls in addition to zombies is a small but good character detail. Decent but not special.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, God. There's nothing sexy about cheese. Put it away.

jokes.text: Frank wakes up: 'Oh. What happened? Where am I?' — he's been asleep in the back office after passing out playing the video game
jokes.setup: Frank has been pushing to finish the video game obsessively
jokes.punchline: He's the one who passed out — mirroring Mac's earlier breakdown — now experiencing the same sleep deprivation consequences
jokes.explanation: The reversal — Frank who judged Mac's weakness now experiencing the same breakdown — is a solid structural callback. 'I think I got PTSD, too' is a good line. Executed competently but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: This is, uh... They took out the kidney, actually, from the fron... A Chinaman. And he did not know how to do it, I'll tell you that much.

jokes.text: Oh, Mac. I think I was too hard on you. I think I got PTSD, too. / Oh, no. We don't have that. / Yeah, I actually slept about ten hours last night, dude, and I feel great. I think we were just suffering from sleep deprivation.
jokes.setup: Frank has a moment of apparent emotional vulnerability — connecting with Mac over shared PTSD
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately deflates it: 'Oh, no. We don't have that.' Then explains it was just sleep deprivation — the whole arc of psychological crisis resolved in one sentence
jokes.explanation: Structurally very satisfying. The episode builds Mac's psychological breakdown as a real character moment, and then Mac pulls the rug out by diagnosing both of them with 'just sleep deprivation.' It's the show's signature anti-growth beat — problems aren't solved, they're simply dismissed. Mac's flat 'Oh, no. We don't have that.' is excellent delivery.

dialogue.line: I love you, Dad!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis

jokes.text: Listen, you like video games? I got you paid for it. You're a great stripper? I got you this gig. And you know what I'm gonna do for you next? I'm gonna reunite you with your daughter.
jokes.setup: Dee is presenting herself as Mike's benefactor and life coach — his 'rock'
jokes.punchline: The crescendo of Dee's good deeds — culminating in reuniting Mike with his estranged daughter — is played completely straight, but we know what's coming given Dee's track record
jokes.explanation: Setup for the episode's climax. Dee's confident 'I'm a rock' energy is well-deployed here as dramatic irony — the audience knows this will end badly.

dialogue.line: This is not sexy! Just take something off! You know, you take something off!

jokes.text: And you can't see any of the blood. / Okay, good.
jokes.setup: Charlie is prepping Dennis before the show
jokes.punchline: The casual mention of 'blood' — from Charlie's earlier nervous back-cutting — is treated as a minor logistics note, not a medical concern
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. The breezy 'you can't see any of the blood / okay, good' as a pre-show checklist item is very Sunny — problems aren't solved, just concealed.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: you might want to check your programs 'cause I'm bad dad now. I'll take you to your goddamn room. I'll bend you over my knee.

jokes.text: What do you think about my prop, hmm? A little kid licking that up there. / Wait, what am I smelling? / Cheese. / Is that made of cheese? / Yeah, yeah. And then I painted the rest with, like, magic marker and stuff. / Oh, Christ. Why did you make a cheese lollipop? It stinks. / For-for my nerves.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks about Charlie's prop for the act
jokes.punchline: Charlie has made a lollipop out of cheese and painted it with magic marker as a 'prop' — and made it because of nerves
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The cheese lollipop is pure Charlie — bizarre, logical to no one but him, made for a reason that makes the situation WORSE rather than better ('for my nerves'). The reveal builds perfectly: prop → kid licking it → smell → 'cheese' → magic marker → 'why?' → 'for my nerves.' Each beat escalates the absurdity. Extremely high character integration: only Charlie would do this. This is the kind of Charlie-specific absurdism that makes the show beloved.

dialogue.speaker: Janie
dialogue.line: Dad? Oh, Janie? Your cock was in my face! Oh, God, I didn't mean to! You're disgusting! My finger touched your asshole!

jokes.text: This, actually, is a real scar, too. And I got a good story behind that. This is, uh... They took out the kidney, actually, from the fron... A Chinaman. And he did not know how to do it, I'll tell you that much.
jokes.setup: Cricket is emceeing the event and riffs on his appearance
jokes.punchline: Cricket's casual aside about an illegal kidney removal by an unlicensed surgeon, delivered mid-emcee patter, is a perfect reminder of Cricket's catastrophic life trajectory
jokes.explanation: Cricket is a walking monument to the show's dark comedy, and his kidney story is exactly the kind of casual horror that makes his character so funny. 'He did not know how to do it, I'll tell you that much' as a deadpan kicker while emceeing a strip show is excellent character work. High character integration — this joke only exists because of Cricket's entire arc.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I got you! I got you. I'm your rock bottom? I'm your rock... That's your rock bottom, sticking your dick in your daughter's face, you son of a bitch.

jokes.text: Cricket was a bad idea, huh? / Yeah. But looks like we got AIDS Dallas Buyers Club McConaughey, not Magic Mike McConaughey. / That is what he looks like.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie realize Cricket was the wrong choice as emcee
jokes.punchline: The McConaughey distinction — 'AIDS Dallas Buyers Club McConaughey vs. Magic Mike McConaughey' — is a precise, funny visual comparison that perfectly captures Cricket's gaunt appearance
jokes.explanation: The McConaughey two-film comparison is a clever, specific observational joke. It earns the laugh by being genuinely precise — not just 'he looks bad' but a specific visual reference that doubles as a commentary on Cricket's tragic decline. 'That is what he looks like' as a flat confirmation is a good beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Wow, Dee, that was dark. That's like the darkest thing you've ever done.

jokes.text: That was the first time that I really thought, 'Hey, I might actually... I might die, and no one's gonna remember.'
jokes.setup: Cricket is rambling mid-emcee about his scar backstory
jokes.punchline: His kidney surgery story pivots to an existential lament — 'no one's gonna remember' — delivered to a room of sorority girls waiting for strippers
jokes.explanation: Cricket's moment of genuine existential reflection mid-emcee of a strip show is the show's dark comedy working at a high level. It's funny but also slightly sad, which is Cricket's zone. The inappropriateness of the setting makes the pathos even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Let's just, uh... let's just get drunk. Let's not talk about trauma. Or deal with any of that shit. stuff it down with some brown.

jokes.text: All right! Let's, uh, keep it movin'. Keepin' it real, keepin' it sexy, and takin' back the power, let's give it up for Daddy and the Boy!
jokes.setup: Cricket has just had a moment of existential despair mid-emcee
jokes.punchline: He snaps back into emcee mode with enthusiastic catchphrases — 'keepin' it sexy, takin' back the power' — as if the dark aside never happened
jokes.explanation: Good tonal whiplash. The pivot from Cricket's despair to 'keepin' it real, keepin' it sexy' works as a character beat. 'Takin' back the power' applied to a strip show is a minor irony joke.

jokes.text: Hey, Boy, let's have a catch. / Over here, Pop. / Hey. Good throw, son. / I love you, Dad! / I love you, too, son. And even though I never said it enough.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie take the stage at the sorority party as 'Daddy and the Boy'
jokes.punchline: Instead of stripping, they're doing a wholesome father-son catch scene — 'I love you, Dad!' — in front of a crowd that came for a strip show
jokes.explanation: The gap between what the audience (and the sorority girls) expected and what they got — emotional father-son reconciliation theater — is excellent cringe comedy. Dennis's total commitment to the emotional narrative ('I never said it enough') while standing in a strip show is very funny. It also ties back to the daddy issues/trauma thread throughout the episode.

jokes.text: Hey, Boy, let's have a catch. / Over here, Pop. / Good throw, son. / I love you, Dad! / I love you, too, son. And even though I never said it enough.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie take the stage as 'Daddy and the Boy' at the sorority strip show
jokes.punchline: Instead of stripping, they begin performing an emotional father-son catch sequence, earnestly enacting a Hallmark-style father-son reconciliation
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's funniest sequences. Dennis and Charlie are supposed to be stripping but instead they're doing sincere father-son emotional reconciliation theater — 'I love you, too, son. And even though I never said it enough' at a sorority strip show is brilliantly wrong. It callbacks Mac's father dream beautifully, and the gap between what the audience (sorority girls) wants and what they're getting is perfect cringe/absurdist comedy. Scores 8+ because it ties the episode's themes together while being genuinely hilarious.

jokes.text: This is super weird. / Hey! Shush. This is our thing. We have the power. You don't talk.
jokes.setup: The crowd is confused and unimpressed by the father-son baseball catch
jokes.punchline: Dennis sternly silences a heckler — 'we have the power, you don't talk' — reasserting authority in a situation where he objectively has no authority
jokes.explanation: Dennis asserting 'we have the power' while bombing in front of sorority girls is perfect Dennis energy — absolute confidence in complete failure. The 'you don't talk' command is especially funny given the situation. High character integration.

jokes.text: It's too hot for baseball. I'm gonna take my clothes off now. I think. / Okay! / Yeah, now we'll take our clothes off. Yeah!
jokes.setup: The father-son act is completely failing; Dennis has dug in defending it
jokes.punchline: 'It's too hot for baseball' as the fictional in-universe excuse to finally take his clothes off — delivered tentatively ('I think') — is a funny, awkward pivot
jokes.explanation: The 'too hot for baseball' justification maintaining the fiction of the act even while abandoning it is a good joke. Dennis's uncertain 'I think' shows genuine disorientation — this confident man now needs crowd validation.

jokes.text: Wait, wait, son, don't. Don't. They're laughing. Don't take your clothes off if they're laughing. We have the power. It's not a joke!
jokes.setup: The crowd finally approves of something (undressing) but Dennis reverses because they're laughing
jokes.punchline: Dennis would rather bomb completely than have his strip act be 'a joke' — his pride overrules the entire point of being there
jokes.explanation: This is Dennis at peak character. He went to a strip show to strip, the crowd is finally responsive, and he STOPS because they're laughing rather than reverentially aroused. 'We have the power' is now a fully tragic mantra. 'It's not a joke!' is the perfect irrational line. His character logic is completely coherent — Dennis cannot accept being mocked — and it makes the moment both hilarious and revealing. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in character specificity and structure.

jokes.text: This is about a father and a son whose relation... / Oh, come on!
jokes.setup: Dennis tries to explain the emotional narrative of the act to the angry crowd
jokes.punchline: He's immediately shouted down before he can finish — the crowd's 'Oh, come on!' perfectly mirrors the audience's feeling
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat. Dennis's interrupted explanation is funny but it's more of a transitional beat than a full joke. The heckle does most of the work.

jokes.text: All right, listen to me. This is it. This is what you were made for. Now you get out there and save the day, soldier.
jokes.setup: The strip show is completely failing; Dee sends Mike out to save it
jokes.punchline: Dee channeling a military commander sending troops into battle — 'this is what you were made for, soldier' — applied to a stripper at a sorority party
jokes.explanation: Good contextual irony — Dee using military/coach language to send a stripper onstage, while PTSD and the military have been themes all episode. Ties the episode's threads together in a funny way.

jokes.text: Dad? / Oh, Janie? / Oh! / Your cock was in my face! / Oh, God, I didn't mean to! I didn't mean to! / You're disgusting! / My finger touched your asshole! / Never talk to me again!
jokes.setup: Mike is stripping; Dee has arranged for his estranged daughter to attend to reunite them
jokes.punchline: Mike's daughter sees him stripping and the reunion becomes a horror of accidental genital contact, escalating rapidly through 'cock in my face' → 'finger in asshole' → permanent estrangement
jokes.explanation: The climax of the episode and the show's signature escalating horror-comedy. The structure is exquisite: the tender reunion setup ('Dad? / Oh, Janie?') immediately destroyed by 'your cock was in my face,' then escalated to 'my finger touched your asshole' — each revelation worse than the last. The escalation is perfectly paced and the cringe is maximized by the fact that Dee ARRANGED this. This is Sunny at its most darkly funny. High impact because it's the episode's comedic peak and delivers on every setup.

jokes.text: I got you! I got you. I'm your rock bottom? I'm your rock... That's your rock bottom, sticking your dick in your daughter's face, you son of a bitch. / Why would you do that?!
jokes.setup: Mike said sex with Dee was his rock bottom; Dee has now orchestrated something far worse
jokes.punchline: Dee triumphantly reclaims her dignity by pointing out that THIS is a real rock bottom — accidentally exposing yourself to your daughter — with furious vindication
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural callback and payoff. The episode's A-plot — Dee not being someone's rock bottom — resolves by Dee engineering something genuinely worse and vindictively claiming victory. 'That's your rock bottom, sticking your dick in your daughter's face' is a great, specific, unhinged line. Dee's triumphant 'I got you!' makes it funnier — she considers this a WIN. High character integration: only Dee would interpret this disaster as personal vindication.

jokes.text: Wow, Dee, that was dark. / That's like the darkest thing you've ever done.
jokes.setup: Dee has just engineered a man accidentally exposing himself to his estranged daughter
jokes.punchline: Even the gang — who do terrible things constantly — are impressed by how dark this was; calling it 'the darkest thing you've ever done' on THIS show is a meaningful distinction
jokes.explanation: Good meta beat — the gang acknowledging the darkness serves as both a character reaction and a slight wink to the audience. 'Darkest thing you've ever done' on Always Sunny is a genuinely high bar. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Whatever. Feel good. I don't want to talk about it.' / Gang: 'You know what we should do? Let's just get drunk.' / 'Let's not talk about trauma. Or deal with any of that shit.' / 'Stuff it down with some brown.'
jokes.setup: Everyone has just experienced something terrible or uncomfortable
jokes.punchline: The gang immediately reverts to their default coping mechanism — 'stuff it down with brown' — the exact phrase Frank used earlier as a critique of their emotional avoidance, now adopted wholesale
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing callback. Frank's earlier pseudo-wisdom about drinking problems away has become the gang's group chant by the end. The episode that supposedly addressed trauma resolves with everyone deciding to use alcohol to avoid processing anything. The structure is satisfying — 'stuff it down with brown' as bookend. This is what the show is about: no growth, only collective denial. The callback elevates what would be a generic ending.

jokes.text: I don't want to talk about my thing. You want to talk about your thing? / No, no, let's not. / You know what we should do? Let's just get drunk. Let's not talk about trauma. Or deal with any of that shit. / Stuff it down with some brown.
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the episode's events, there's a moment where the gang could address their actual problems
jokes.punchline: They immediately agree to drink and avoid all of it; Frank reprises 'stuff it down with brown' — the episode's alternative to actual therapy
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode cap. 'Stuff it down with brown' as a callback to Frank's coping philosophy, now unanimously endorsed by the whole gang after a catastrophic episode, is satisfying structural comedy. The anti-growth resolution is very Sunny. Good but not exceptional — it's a grace note rather than a punchline.

tmdb_overview: Dee dates a male stripper and tries to prove her worth after learning she's his "rock bottom." Elsewhere: Mac and Frank get sucked into a VR war game, leading Mac to develop a case PTSD.
